Abstract 1

2

Objectives: To develop the Global Diet Quality Score (GDQS) for children 24-59-months and 3

evaluate its performance in predicting outcomes related to nutrient adequacy and diet-related 4

non-communicable disease (NCD) risk. 5

6

Background: The GDQS is a food-based metric developed and validated for capturing diets' 7

contributions to nutrient adequacy and NCD risk among adult men and nonpregnant and 8

nonlactating women >15 years globally. Despite the importance of ensuring healthy diets in 9

preschool children and the need for systematic monitoring, no food-based metrics exist that 10

holistically measure diet quality among 24-59-month-old children in diverse populations. 11

12

Methods: We developed candidate versions of the GDQS for children 24-59 months by adapting 13

the gram cut-offs used in adults to account for children’s lower energy requirements. Using 14

dietary datasets from Bangladesh, Burkina Faso, China, Ethiopia, Mexico, UK, and USA, we 15

evaluated candidate versions’ performance in predicting energy-adjusted nutrient intakes and 16

adequacy, nutritional biomarkers, and overweight using Spearman’s correlation and 17

multivariable-adjusted regression models, and statistically compared performance of the 18

strongest candidate with that of the Minimum Dietary Diversity–Women (MDD-W) indicator 19

and Global Dietary Recommendations (GDR) score. 20

21

Results: The GDQS exhibited significant (p<0.05) positive correlations with energy-adjusted 22

intakes of protein, fiber, and most micronutrients in most datasets; significant negative 23

correlations with added sugar and saturated fat in two datasets; and inconsistent correlations with 24

monounsaturated and polyunsaturated fat. In multivariable-adjusted models, the GDQS, MDD- 25

W, and GDR were positively associated with serum folate in Ethiopia (and the GDQS was in the 26

UK), and the GDR was positively associated with HDL-cholesterol in China (p<0.05). The 27

GDQS was more strongly associated with the mean probability of adequacy of 8 nutrients than 28

the GDR in two datasets, while the MDD-W outperformed the GDQS in three datasets (p<0.05). 29

30

Conclusion: The GDQS is a useful metric for measuring diet quality among 24-59-month-old 31

children in diverse populations. 32

33

Introduction 36

37

The first five years of life is a critical period for child growth and development. Inadequate 38

nutrient intake during this period can result in various forms of undernutrition and micronutrient 39

deficiencies, leading to increased mortality and morbidity in the short term, as well as long-term 40

consequences such as developmental faltering, lower academic achievement and future earnings, 41

and a higher risk of non-communicable diseases (NCDs)1-4. Excessive intake of refined 42

carbohydrates, ultra-processed foods, and sugary beverages, and low fruit and vegetable 43

consumption contribute to childhood obesity, which is associated with increased oxidative stress, 44

low-grade inflammation, insulin resistance, and dyslipidemia; early life metabolic dysfunctions 45

further contribute to increased risk of type 2 diabetes, non-alcoholic fatty liver disease, and 46

cardiovascular diseases in middle childhood and early adulthood5-10. In 2022, an estimated 148 47

million children under five globally were stunted (height-for-age z-score <-2 standard deviations 48

(SD)), 45 million were wasted (weight-for-height z-score <-2SD), 37 million were overweight 49

(body mass index (BMI)-for-age z-score >2 SD) and 372 million had major micronutrient 50

deficiencies including iron, zinc, and/or vitamin A deficiencies11,12. Considering the significant 51

global burden of dietary inadequacies and excesses and their impacts on child health and 52

development, monitoring children's diet quality is crucial for informing nutrition policies and 53

programs worldwide7. 54

55

Diet quality metrics are tools for assessing and monitoring population diet quality. Several 56

metrics have been utilized to measure diet quality of children 24-59 months of age, such as the 57

Dietary Diversity Score (DDS), Minimum Dietary Diversity for Women (MDD-W), and Healthy 58


<!-- Page 6 -->


6

Eating Index (HEI)13-17 The DDS and MDD-W are calculated based on a simple count of food 59

groups consumed within the previous 24 hours and focus on assessing dietary diversity (a proxy 60

for nutrient adequacy)13,14. The HEI measures a degree of adherence to the U.S. Dietary 61

Guidelines and has been adapted for use in numerous other countries; while the HEI-2020 is 62

appropriate for understanding both nutrient adequacy and NCD risk in children 2 years and 63

older, it requires detailed nutrient intake data that may be challenging to collect in low- and 64

middle income settings (LMICs)15,16. Given the limitations of existing metrics, there is a need to 65

develop a simple, food-based metric of diet quality for use in children 2-5 years of age that can 66

capture the contribution of diet to both nutrient adequacy and NCD risk. Validating such a metric 67

across low-, middle-, and high-income countries is also essential, as dietary patterns vary 68

enormously across cultures and contexts18. 69

70

To our knowledge, the Global Diet Quality Score (GDQS) is currently the only food-based 71

metric that has been developed and extensively validated to holistically capture nutrient 72

adequacy and dietary NCD risk among adult men and non-pregnant nonlactating women of 73

reproductive age (NPNL WRA) (15 years and older) in diverse settings19-28 . The GDQS is 74

readily assessed in population surveys using the GDQS app, which has been validated in primary 75

data collection29,30. These factors render the GDQS an attractive candidate for adaptation to other 76

age groups. This study therefore sought to adapt and validate the GDQS for use in children 24-59 77

months of age as part of a broader effort to develop GDQS metrics for children 2-14 years. 78

Datasets 82

83

We analyzed seven cross-sectional datasets that included information on food and nutrient 84

intakes for children aged 24-59 months. These included four nationally representative datasets: 85

China Health and Nutrition Survey 1997–2011 (n=1330), Mexico National Health and Nutrition 86

Survey 2012 and 2017 (n=2098), UK National Diet and Nutrition Survey, 2008-2019, (n=2330), 87

and US National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey, 2017-2018 (n=410)31-35. The three 88

subnational cross-sectional surveys included in this analysis were conducted in Bangladesh 89

(n=460), Burkina Faso (n=955), and Ethiopia (n=1540)36-38. Key characteristics of each survey 90

are provided in Table 1. 91

92

Quantitative 24-hour dietary recall surveys were conducted in Burkina Faso, China, Ethiopia, 93

Mexico, and USA, in which respondents or caregivers estimated all foods and beverages 94

consumed during the 24-hour reference period. For each dataset, two days of repeat 24-hour 95

recall data were available for a subsample of the population. In the UK, a quantitative food diary 96

was used in which respondents or caregivers recorded all foods and beverages consumed over 97

four 24-hour periods within a seven-day range. In Bangladesh, a weighed observation method 98

was employed over two days (typically one weekday and one weekend), during which 99

enumerators observed and weighed all foods and beverages consumed over a 12-hour period, 100

supplemented by recall of any items consumed outside this timeframe. Detailed information on 101

sampling methods, assessments, and population characteristics for each survey are available in 102

prior publications31-39,. 103

Selection of outcomes for validation of metrics 111

112

We selected outcomes related to dietary nutrient adequacy and diet-related NCD risk available in 113

each dataset (Table 1). Outcomes primarily related to nutrient adequacy included dietary intake 114

of protein, calcium, iron, zinc, vitamin A, thiamine, and vitamin B12; a derived measure of 115

overall dietary nutrient adequacy; and serum ferritin, transferrin, folate, and vitamin B12. 116

Outcomes primarily related to NCD risk included dietary intake of monounsaturated, 117

polyunsaturated, and saturated fatty acids (MUFA, PUFA, and SFA), as well as fiber and added 118

sugar; serum lipids (total cholesterol, LDL, HDL, and triglycerides), glucose, and insulin; and 119

HbA1c measured in whole blood. One binary anthropometric NCD-related outcome was also 120

included (child overweight or obesity, defined as BMI-for-age z-score >2) considering 121

associations between dietary risks, childhood overweight, and its contribution to metabolic 122

disfunction5-9,40. 123

124

Overall nutrient adequacy was defined as the mean probability of adequacy of eight nutrients of 125

key importance in LMICs, seven of which were previously included in calculating overall 126

nutrient adequacy in prior work to develop and validate the GDQS for adults (fiber, calcium, 127


<!-- Page 9 -->


9

iron, zinc, vitamin A, folate, and vitamin B12) and one nutrient (thiamine) which was added 128

considering growing recognition of its importance in LMICs19,41. Probability of adequacy of each 129

nutrient was based on predicted usual intakes (derivation described below). 130

Statistical analysis 1: deriving usual nutrient intakes and probability of adequacy 132

133

Nutrient intakes were expressed as estimated usual intakes predicted using the NCI method in 134

SAS v.9.4, adjusted for four model covariates: age, sex, sequence of dietary assessment day, and 135

weekday vs. weekend day42. For each nutrient, we applied the full probability method to estimate 136

each child’s probability of adequacy in reference to Harmonized Average Requirements (ARs) 137

and coefficients of variation (CVs) proposed by Allen et al. assuming dataset-specific iron 138

bioavailability factors based on prevailing dietary patterns: 16% for US, UK, and China; 10% for 139

Bangladesh; and 5% for Burkina Faso, Ethiopia, and Mexico43. For fiber, we estimated an AR by 140

dividing the adequate intake level by 1.30 and assuming a CV of 15%, adapting an approach 141

proposed by Allen et al for nutrients lacking ARs. 142

Process of developing the GDQS metric for children 24-59 months of age 144

145

We used the GDQS previously developed and validated for adults as the starting point for 146

developing the GDQS for use in children 24-59 months of age19. For consistency with the adult 147

version of the metric, we retained the original 25 GDQS food groups as well as the point values 148

used to score categories of consumed amounts of each food group (low, moderate, high, and very 149

high). Foods consumed in each dataset were coded according to GDQS food groups following 150


<!-- Page 10 -->


10

published guidance19. Breastmilk (quantitative consumption data of which was included in the 151

Bangladesh datasets) and infant formula (included in all other datasets) were included in the 152

high-fat dairy group. Given the potentially important contribution of breastmilk to diets of 153

children aged 24-59 months, eight children from the USA for which breastmilk consumption was 154

reported without quantification were excluded from the analysis. 155

156

Metric development focused on adapting the gram-per-day cutoffs used to score categories of 157

consumed amounts of GDQS food groups in adults to children 24-59 months of age19. These 158

include a lower cutoff used to differentiate low and moderate consumption, an upper cutoff used 159

to differentiate moderate and high consumption, and, for one food group (high-fat dairy), a third 160

cutoff used to differentiate high and very high consumption. 161

162

Considering lower energy requirements for children 2-5 years, first, we adjusted the adult cutoffs 163

based on the ratio of average energy requirements of boys and girls aged 24-59 months to those 164

of NPNL WRA (the demographic for which the GDQS was originally designed) using Tables 165

4.2, 4.3, 4.6, 5.7, and 5.8 of the report on the 2004 FAO/WHO/UNU Expert Consultation on 166

Human Energy Requirements44. For boys and girls, we assumed a moderate physical activity 167

level and an equal number of boys and girls in each age group, resulting in an average 168

requirement of 1146 kcal/day (rounded to 1100 to acknowledge imprecision in the underlying 169

estimates). The average energy requirement for adult women was calculated as 2289 kcal/day 170

(rounded to 2300). This resulted in a factor of 1100/2300=0.48 used to scale down the adult 171

gram-per-day cutoffs for all food groups except red meat and high-fat dairy, for which the upper 172

and third cutoffs were retained, respectively, to limit the number of children classified to high 173


<!-- Page 11 -->


11

consumption of red meat and very high consumption of high-fat dairy (the GDQS assigns 0 174

points to the highest red meat and high-fat dairy consumption categories to penalize excessive 175

consumption of these food groups as an NCD risk factor, but this risk was assumed to be less 176

deleterious for young children than adults). 177

178

Beginning with the initial scaled-down version of the metric (candidate V1), we developed 179

candidate metrics V2-V5 by incorporating further adjustments to the food group scoring cutoffs 180

(apart from the liquid oils group which was not modified further). Adjustments were aimed at 181

improving the operational feasibility of collecting metric data from populations as well as 182

achieving a more even population distribution of food group consumption categories. 183

184

• V2: Candidate metric V2 was developed by more closely aligning the food group scoring 185

cutoffs with an existing set of cutoffs employed by the GDQS app29,30. The app uses 10 cubes 186

of pre-specified volumes (each of which corresponds to a specific gram amount for each food 187

group) to assess the amount of each food group consumed by participants. V2 modified the 188

lower and upper cutoffs of V1 so that they aligned with the nearest-sized cube used in the 189

GDQS app without exceeding the cutoffs used for corresponding food groups in V1. By 190

more closely aligning food group scoring cutoffs between the metric and the GDQS app, we 191

aimed to improve the operational feasibility of collecting standardized data on the metric 192

from study populations. 193

194

• V3: In all seven analytical datasets, we applied V1 to calculate each child’s point values for 195

each GDQS food group. Upon examination of the resulting distribution of children in the 196


<!-- Page 12 -->


12

low, moderate, high and very high consumption categories of each food group, we observed 197

that the moderate consumption category was relatively underrepresented. Therefore, V3 used 198

the lower cutoffs of V2 and modified the upper cutoffs so that they aligned with the next 199

largest GDQS app cube size. This allowed V3 to achieve a more even population distribution 200

of consumption categories while attempting to retain the operational advantage of V2. 201

202

• V4 and V5: Candidate metrics V4 and V5 used the upper cutoffs of V2 and V3, respectively, 203

and extended the lower cutoffs downward to capture non-consumption. This way, V4 and V5 204

provided a further operational advantage to V2 and V3 by eliminating the need to quantify 205

consumption within the lowest category when collecting data to calculate the metric (in other 206

words, if a participant did not consume a food group at all, it could automatically be scored 207

as low consumption). V5 also attempted to retain the advantage of V3 in providing a more 208

even population distribution of consumption categories. 209

Statistical analysis 2: informing selection of the most suitable candidate metric 215

216

To inform selection of the most suitable candidate metric, we calculated Spearman’s correlations 217

between metrics V1-V5 and all available continuous outcomes in all seven country datasets 218

(Supplemental Tables 2-4). In this analysis, and in subsequent correlation analyses to evaluate 219

13

performance of the selected candidate metric, nutrient intakes and overall nutrient adequacy were 220

adjusted for predicted usual total energy intake using the residual method45. 221

For most outcomes, candidates V1, V3, and V5 displayed slightly stronger correlations in the 222

expected directions (defined as positive for nutrient adequacy-related outcomes and negative for 223

NCD-related outcomes except MUFA and PUFA, fiber, and HDL-C) than V2 and V4. Candidate 224

V5 displayed the most numerous statistically-significant results, including strong correlations in 225

expected directions with energy-adjusted overall nutrient adequacy, most nutrient intakes, and 226

nutritional biomarkers including serum vitamin B12 and a marginally significant correlation (p = 227

0.05) with LDL-C in the UK dataset; serum folate in the UK and Ethiopia; and serum HDL-C, 228

triglycerides, and insulin in China. Based on these results, and considering V5’s aforementioned 229

operational advantages, V5 was identified as the most suitable version of the GDQS metric for 230

further evaluation among children 24-59 months of age. 231

Statistical analysis 3: evaluating performance of the GDQS and comparison metrics in children 246

24-59 months of age 247

248

Considering GDQS as an ordinal scale, correlations between GDQS with energy-adjusted 249

nutrient intakes, nutrient adequacy, and biomarkers were estimated using Spearman correlations 250

in each dataset46.   We used multivariable linear regression models to determine estimated 251

marginal means (EMMs) of each outcome within GDQS quintiles, EMMs in terms of a 1 SD 252

difference in GDQS, and statistical significance of trends in EMMs across GDQS quintiles, 253

assuming independence, linearity of the conditional distribution and homoscedasticity of the 254

error term. We also ran multivariable logistic regression models to estimate covariate-adjusted 255

odds ratios (ORs) and linear trends for the binary outcome of overweight or obese (BMI-for-age 256

z-score >2). Models were adjusted for age, sex, predicted usual total energy intake45 (for nutrient 257

intake and overall nutrient adequacy outcomes), and the following potential confounders where 258

data were available: urban vs. rural locality (adjusted in China, Ethiopia, and Mexico datasets), 259

education level of the household head or mother (adjusted in Ethiopia and Mexico), occupation 260

of the household head or the mother (adjusted in Bangladesh, Ethiopia, and Mexico), and 261

measures of household socioeconomic status such as household income and household socio- 262

economic index whichever available for the datasets (adjusted in Bangladesh, Mexico, and UK). 263

264

15

Correlation and regression analyses were repeated for two existing comparison metrics to 265

provide a benchmark for GDQS performance. These metrics were the MDD-W (which we 266

scored as a continuous indicator ranging from 0 to 10) and the Global Dietary Recommendation 267

(GDR) score (which measures adherence to WHO dietary recommendations that prevent NCD 268

risk and ranges from 0 to 18). The components and scoring methods of the MDD-W and GDR 269

are provided in published references17,47. To score the GDR in each country, we used the foods 270

represented in the Diet Quality Questionnaire (DQ-Q) for that country to produce statistics 271

representative of the method for collecting data needed to calculate the GDR that would typically 272

be used in practice. We excluded scoring the GDR in the UK dataset as no DQ-Q was available 273

for that country. In some datasets, the MDD-W and GDR were analyzed using quartiles due to 274

limited variation in metric scores. Statistical comparisons of linear trends in EMMs and ORs 275

Discussion 403

404

In this study, we address a global gap in monitoring the diet quality of children aged 24-59 405

months by developing and validating a food-based diet quality metric, the GDQS, for children 406

aged 24-59 months in diverse contexts. In general, the GDQS showed significant positive 407

associations with energy-adjusted intakes of nutrients related to nutrient adequacy and negative 408

associations with nutrients related to NCD risk. The GDQS tended to perform better in 409

comparison with the GDR in predicting macro- and micronutrient intakes and mean probability 410

of nutrient adequacy. In contrast, the performance of the GDQS and MDD-W in predicting 411

nutrient intakes varied across nutrients and countries. In predicting nutrients related to NCD risk, 412

performance of the GDQS and GDR were comparable, while the MDD-W performed less well 413

compared to the GDQS. We observed no significant associations between the GDQS and 414

overweight or nutritional biomarkers except for serum folate, which showed a significant 415

positive association with the GDQS, GDR, and MDD-W in Ethiopia, although pairwise 416

comparisons between these associations were not significant. 417

418

We found substantial variation in diet quality of children aged 24-59 months across country 419

datasets18. Consistent with previous studies, we found children in high-income countries such as 420

the UK and the USA had lower diet quality (reflected by lower mean GDQS) while LMICs like 421

Bangladesh, Burkina Faso, China, Ethiopia, and Mexico had comparatively high diet quality 422

(higher mean GDQS)19,29. These differences are partly driven by variation in consumption of 423

unhealthy food groups, such as processed foods and sugar-sweetened beverages, which are 424


<!-- Page 22 -->


22

broadly influenced by the levels of socioeconomic development in these countries. For example, 425

highly developed countries like the UK and the USA are among the top consumers of ultra- 426

processed foods, whereas LMICs are shifting toward increased processed food consumption due 427

to ongoing industrialization and globalization of food markets but have not yet reached 428

consumption levels seen in high-income countries48,49. Furthermore, local cultural practices play 429

a major role in shaping healthy diet choices; for example, injera, a staple food in Ethiopian 430

cuisine which is central to Ethiopian culture, is traditionally made from teff, a whole grain50,51. 431

432

Our results also showed that among young children in diverse settings, the GDQS was positively 433

associated with energy-adjusted intakes of nutrients linked to nutrient adequacy and negatively 434

associated with nutrients related to NCD risk, with notable exceptions of MUFA and PUFA, 435

which are consistent with our previous findings in validating the GDQS for use in adults19. 436

Specifically, the GDQS showed positive associations with MUFA and PUFA intake in LMIC 437

datasets such as Bangladesh, and negative associations in high-income country datasets such as 438

the UK and the USA. This may partly be explained by variations in the main sources of dietary 439

fats and cooking oils that contribute to MUFA and PUFA intakes in these countries52,53. For 440

example, in LMICs where populations still largely subsist on plant-based diets, vegetable oils 441

remain major sources of MUFA and PUFA (70-80%)53,54. Liquid oils are coded positively in the 442

GDQS and may thus contribute to positive associations in these countries. On the other hand, 443

negative associations between the GDQS and MUFA and PUFA intake in high-income countries 444

may arise from food systems largely consisting of processed foods55-57. As a result, individuals in 445

these countries may tend to replace whole food sources of PUFAs with ultra-processed foods or 446

other fat sources that may be lower in PUFAs, even when aiming for a healthier diet. 447


<!-- Page 23 -->


23

448

Furthermore, we found no associations between the GDQS and biomarkers in this age group 449

except positive associations with serum folate in Ethiopia and the UK datasets. This finding is 450

consistent with a parallel analysis of GDQS performance among children aged 5-9 years58, and 451

prior analysis of Ethiopian men and women59. In contrast to our findings, longitudinal studies 452

have reported significant negative associations between the GDQS (measured using food- 453

frequency questionnaires) and fasting plasma glucose, insulin, and insulin resistance in Indian 454

children 9.5-13.5 years of age and anthropometric measures of adiposity in Mexican children 4-7 455

years of age60,61. Largely null associations between diet metrics and both nutritional biomarkers 456

and overweight observed in the current analysis may be attributed to the cross-sectional design 457

and the fact that metrics were calculated using dietary data from relatively short reference 458

periods. These factors affected our ability to capture outcomes with longer latency periods (such 459

as overweight) and that incur natural day-to-day variation and measurement error (such as 460

nutrient intake and nutritional biomarkers)62,63. Furthermore, while measures of nutrition status 461

are inherently influenced by various biological factors that render them imperfect proxies for 462

dietary intake, associations may be particularly obscured in young children, whose metabolism is 463

significantly oriented toward growth and development and which introduces additional 464

extraneous variation as a result4,44,64. Therefore, in future studies, associations between diet 465

quality and NCD biomarkers should be explored over time in longitudinal cohort datasets. 466

467

While comparing the performances of the metrics, the MDD-W outperformed the GDQS in 468

predicting overall nutrient adequacy in Bangladesh, Burkina Faso, and Ethiopia. As noted in 469

prior comparative analyses of the GDQS and MDD-W among adults in diverse LMICs, the 470


<!-- Page 24 -->


24

MDD-W has an inherent advantage in predicting nutrient adequacy given that the metric gives 471

positive scores to all foods (all of which contain nutrients)19. In relatively impoverished 472

populations including rural Ethiopian adults, the simplicity of the MDD-W’s design appeared 473

particularly adept at capturing minimum dietary diversity (while the GDQS’ more nuanced 474

scoring system instead added “noise”)22,59. However, these analyses also noted the MDD-W’s 475

limited ability to predict aspects of diet-related NCD risk compared to GDQS in diverse 476

setting20,23-28,65, which have become increasingly important to monitor in LMIC populations 477

considering global nutrition transition and triple burden of malnutrition including undernutrition, 478

overnutrition, and micronutrient deficiencies in these contexts26,66.  On the other hand, the GDQS 479

significantly outperformed the GDR in predicting overall nutrient adequacy in two countries, 480

which may be explained by the GDR’s focus on capturing adherence to dietary guidelines for 481

preventing NCDs. 482

483

The choice of diet metric to use in a given research or programmatic situation should consider its 484

validity for assessing pertinent aspects of diet quality in the population of interest. With 485

adaptation of the GDQS to children 24-59 months (and older, as described in the other articles in 486

this Supplemental Issue), the metric is currently uniquely positioned as the only diet quality 487

metric designed and extensively validated to simultaneously assess both nutrient adequacy and 488

NCD risk across diverse country contexts and age groups58,60,61. The choice of metric should also 489

consider its feasibility in data collection or secondary analysis. The GDQS’ food-based design 490

offers a significant operational advantage in LMICs where food composition data may be 491

lacking. The metric can be calculated using quantitative dietary data collected using a variety of 492

methods (e.g., quantitative 24-hour recall, FFQ, or diet record) in secondary data analysis. Also, 493


<!-- Page 25 -->


25

the GDQS is readily assessed in primary data collection using the GDQS app, a user-friendly 494

means of collecting standardized GDQS data in population surveys that does not require 495

interviewer training, is available in several languages, and can be easily adapted to different 496

contexts through translation and inclusion of new foods29,30. 497

498

This study was strengthened by the expansiveness of its scope, which involved comparative 499

validation of three diet metrics against a range of diet and nutritional outcomes relevant to both 500

nutrient adequacy and NCD risk across six low-, middle-, and high income countries. Key 501

limitations mentioned previously were the dependence on cross-sectional datasets (which 502

inherently limited our ability to infer causal relationships) and data from short-term dietary 503

assessments (which limited our ability to capture long-term effects of diet, which is particularly 504

important for understanding relationships with between diet and biochemical and anthropometric 505

measures of nutrition status). Furthermore, although we adjusted our analyses for 506

sociodemographic factors, residual confounding is possible, as is unmeasured confounding by 507

potentially important factors such as physical activity and infections which were not accounted 508

for due to a lack of data, and should be considered in future research, specifically examining 509

relationships between the GDQS and nutrition status in this age group67. 510

511

Conclusion 512

513

We adapted the GDQS, a food-based metric of diet quality previously developed for use in 514

adults, to children 24-59 months of age. GDQS for children aged 24-59 months predicted both 515

energy-adjusted intakes of macronutrients and micronutrients relevant to nutrient adequacy and 516


<!-- Page 26 -->


26

NCD risk, and mean probability of nutrient adequacy in six low-, middle, and high-income 517

country datasets. These results support and are supported by findings from other articles in this 518

Supplemental Issue examining the GDQS’ validity among children in older age groups. In light 519

of the GDQS’ performance, holistic approach, simplicity, and feasibility for integration in an 520

existing data collection platform (the GDQS app), we propose the GDQS as a useful tool for diet 521

quality monitoring among children in programs and research globally. 522
